26-4.title: India does not require server registration, but the platform must follow the IT Rules and the data-protection law
26-4.inPlainWords: India does not require a website to register its server. A platform must comply with the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021: publish the terms, appoint a grievance officer, and act on a takedown order. A telecom or internet service provider needs a licence, but a website owner does not need a telecom licence.
26-4.benefit: The IT Act, 2000 gives an intermediary a safe harbour if it follows the due-diligence rules. The 2021 Rules require a grievance officer, a monthly compliance report and a response within a set time. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires consent and security for personal data. CERT-In's directions require incident reporting within six hours. A payment gateway has separate RBI rules.
26-4.cost: Compliance costs time and, for a large platform, a compliance team. A small blog mostly needs a privacy policy and a grievance contact.
26-4.caveats: A platform cannot claim safe harbour if it knowingly hosts unlawful content. A server outside India does not avoid Indian law if the service targets Indian users. A 'licence' sold by an agent is not a substitute for compliance.
26-4.sources: Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>

26-9.inPlainWords: If you host user content, publish a grievance process and act on a valid takedown notice or a court order. The IT Rules, 2021 give an intermediary a safe harbour only if it follows the due-diligence rules and acts on an order. Do not ignore a notice, and do not remove content merely because someone objects without evidence. Tell the seller and keep a record.
26-9.benefit: The IT Act, 2000, section 79, gives an intermediary a safe harbour if it does not initiate the transmission and follows the due-diligence rules. The IT Rules, 2021 require a grievance officer, a response within a set time, and action on a court order or a government direction. A platform that knows of unlawful content and does nothing can lose the safe harbour. India does not have the 15-day restore rule described in the source edition; a takedown should follow the notice and the law.
26-9.cost: No cost for a small platform beyond a policy page and a grievance contact. A legal review costs money.
26-9.caveats: Do not remove content just because a rights holder demands it; ask for the order or the evidence. Preserve the notice and your response. A false or malicious notice can be a defamation or a civil wrong.
26-9.sources: Information Technology Act, 2000 (section 79). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
26-9.title: Respond promptly to a takedown notice: India has no 15-day restoration rule, so act on the order and keep the record

26-1.title: Never hold the buyer's money and pass it on later: in India that is a payment business and needs RBI authorisation
26-1.inPlainWords: If your platform collects the buyer's money into its own account and later pays the seller, you are running a payment system, not a marketplace. In India that needs authorisation from the Reserve Bank under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, and the customer's money has to sit in an escrow account with a scheduled commercial bank, not in your working capital. The clean design is a licensed payment aggregator or gateway that collects from the buyer and settles to the seller, with you taking a commission and never touching the principal.
26-1.benefit: The Reserve Bank's guidelines for payment aggregators and payment gateways treat an entity that handles funds in the payment flow as a payment aggregator, which needs authorisation under the 2007 Act. A non-bank aggregator must keep the funds in an escrow account with a scheduled commercial bank and follow a board-approved settlement policy. A marketplace that only matches buyer and seller and never holds the money is outside that regime. An unauthorised payment system can be stopped by the Reserve Bank and the money in it frozen.
26-1.cost: A licensed aggregator charges a percentage of each transaction. Building your own escrow arrangement and authorisation costs far more than that fee.
26-1.caveats: Do not use your current account as a pass-through. Do not hold settlement back to smooth your cash flow: that is exactly the conduct the rules forbid. Have the money flow checked by a lawyer before you launch.
26-1.sources: Reserve Bank of India, regulation of payment aggregators and payment gateways. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

26-2.title: India has no licence for a paid website: the permission attaches to what the site does, not to whether it charges
26-2.inPlainWords: There is no value-added telecommunications licence in India, and no general licence for a website that charges its users. What you need depends on the activity: a GST registration if you sell, an authorised payment partner if you collect money, a marketplace that follows the e-commerce rules, and the ordinary company and municipal registrations. A free site needs the same domain and hosting as a paid one, but no content licence. Some activities do carry their own permission: news, film, gaming, lending, insurance and health claims each have a regulator.
26-2.benefit: The Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Intermediary Guidelines Rules, 2021 regulate platforms as intermediaries, and the safe harbour depends on due diligence rather than on a licence fee. Business registration runs through the GST portal and the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and a shop needs a municipal trade licence. Telecom licensing by the Department of Telecommunications covers telecom and internet service providers, not a website. Sector regulators license the activity: the Reserve Bank for lending and payments, SEBI for securities, IRDAI for insurance.
26-2.cost: Domain and hosting are the real cost. GST registration is free, and a company registration and a trade licence carry fees.
26-2.caveats: A licence offered to a small site by an agency is usually unnecessary. Ask a professional about the specific activity. Do not assume that charging money is what triggers regulation.
26-2.sources: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Goods and Services Tax portal. <https://www.gst.gov.in/>

26-3.title: Live streaming needs no cultural licence in India, but it does need the rights, a grievance officer and care with the content
26-3.inPlainWords: India has no state-issued online-culture licence and no permit to distribute audiovisual content on the internet. If you stream your own content you are its publisher, and if you host other people's streams you are an intermediary under the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Rules of 2021. You need the music and performance rights, a grievance officer and a published policy, and you must act on a court order or a government blocking direction. A ticketed public event may also need a local permission and a noise or timing clearance.
26-3.benefit: The Intermediary Guidelines Rules, 2021 require due diligence, a grievance officer, a periodic compliance report for a significant social media intermediary, and action within 36 hours of a court order or a government notification. Part III of the same Rules applies to a publisher of news and current affairs and to a publisher of online curated content, with self-classification and a grievance mechanism. Copyright in the music, the film and the performance is a separate permission from the rights holder.
26-3.cost: The rights licences are the main cost. A grievance officer and a policy page are not.
26-3.caveats: Do not stream a concert, a match or a film without the rights. Do not assume the content rules stop at the internet. Keep a record of every takedown and every order.
26-3.sources: Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code Rules, 2021. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

26-5.title: If others sell on your platform, verify each seller, display their details and keep records for 180 days
26-5.inPlainWords: A marketplace has to verify a seller's identity and contact details before the seller lists, display the seller's name, address and contact on the listing, and appoint a grievance officer. Under the Intermediary Guidelines Rules, 2021 an intermediary must keep information and records about its users, including a user who has closed the account, for 180 days for an investigation. Tax law and the Companies Act, 2013 can require a longer retention. Keep the listings, the terms and the correspondence, and re-verify a seller whose details change.
26-5.benefit: The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 place the verification and display duties on a marketplace e-commerce entity and make it answerable in defined situations for a seller's failure. The Intermediary Guidelines Rules, 2021 require 180 days of retention of user information and records. A registered seller must display the GST registration, and the platform's records must match the invoices it facilitates. A platform that does not verify can be treated as the seller in a consumer complaint.
26-5.cost: A verification process and a record system cost staff time. A compliance failure costs much more.
26-5.caveats: Do not rely on a self-declaration alone; keep the document you checked. Do not delete a seller's records when the seller leaves. A seller's fake address becomes the platform's problem in a consumer case.
26-5.sources: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Intermediary Guidelines Rules, 2021. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Goods and Services Tax portal. <https://www.gst.gov.in/>

26-6.title: You must moderate user content and act on orders: India's safe harbour depends on it, not on a promise of immunity
26-6.inPlainWords: Publish the rules users must follow, a privacy policy and the contact of a grievance officer, and act on complaints. Under section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 a platform keeps its safe harbour only if it does not initiate the transmission and follows the due-diligence rules; when a court order or a government notification comes, the content must be disabled within 36 hours. Illegal material such as a sexual abuse image, a threat or an offence should be removed and reported to cybercrime.gov.in or the 1930 helpline and, where the law requires it, to the police.
26-6.benefit: Section 79 protects an intermediary from liability for third-party content if the conditions are met. The Intermediary Guidelines Rules, 2021 set out the due-diligence duties, the grievance officer, the 36-hour action on an order and the option of voluntary user verification. A platform that knows of unlawful content and does nothing can lose the protection and face action under the Information Technology Act and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal and the 1930 helpline are the reporting route for a cyber offence.
26-6.cost: A moderation queue and a grievance officer are the cost. A legal notice or a prosecution costs far more.
26-6.caveats: Do not remove content merely because someone objects; ask for an order or for evidence. Do not promise users that the platform is not responsible for content. Preserve the notice and your response.
26-6.sources: Information Technology Act, 2000, section 79. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Intermediary Guidelines Rules, 2021. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>

26-7.title: India has no general real-name rule: you may require a verified phone or email, but not a full identity mandate
26-7.inPlainWords: There is no general law in India that forces a user to give a real name before posting or chatting. You can require a verified mobile number or email at sign-up as a condition of your service, and you should say so in your terms and in the privacy notice. The Intermediary Guidelines Rules, 2021 require a significant social media intermediary to offer voluntary verification with a visible mark, and to be able to identify the first originator of information when a court or an authorised agency orders it. Collecting more identity than you need creates a duty under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
26-7.benefit: The Rules of 2021 provide for voluntary user verification, a verification mark and traceability of the first originator on an order. They do not create a universal real-name requirement. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires a lawful purpose, consent and data minimisation, and a breach of those duties is enforced by the Data Protection Board. A phone-number check is a business choice and a contract term, enforceable under the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
26-7.cost: An OTP check costs a few paise per verification. Storing identity documents costs money in security and compliance.
26-7.caveats: Do not collect an identity document you do not need. Do not publish a user's real name without consent. A verification mark must mean something, so do not sell it.
26-7.sources: Intermediary Guidelines Rules, 2021. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Indian Contract Act, 1872. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

26-8.title: Minors and money: India sets no age-band tipping caps, but the data law changes what you may do with a child's account
26-8.inPlainWords: India does not ban live-streaming accounts for under-16s and does not set tipping caps by age band. What it does have is a data rule: under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 a child is anyone under 18, processing a child's data needs verifiable parental consent, and behavioural advertising directed at a child is prohibited. A minor's agreement is void under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, so a large tip or purchase by a child can be reversed. Set your own age gate, a spend limit and a visible refund route, and publish them.
26-8.benefit: Section 9 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires verifiable parental consent before processing a child's personal data and bars tracking and behavioural advertising directed at children. A minor's agreement is void under section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which is why a payment made by a child can be recovered. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the Central Consumer Protection Authority's guidelines on dark patterns apply to how you design a prompt that nudges a user to spend.
26-8.cost: An age check and a refund policy cost engineering time. A chargeback and a regulator's notice cost more.
26-8.caveats: A self-declared date of birth is not parental consent. Do not design a top-up prompt aimed at a child. Keep the refund route simple and visible.
26-8.sources: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Indian Contract Act, 1872. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>

26-10.title: Moving personal data out of India: the 2023 Act allows it unless the government restricts the destination, and payment data has its own rule
26-10.inPlainWords: Hosting abroad is a cross-border transfer. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 a data fiduciary may transfer personal data outside India unless the Central Government has restricted transfer to a specified country or territory by notification. There is no adequacy assessment, certification or standard-contract filing of the kind some other regimes use. Sector rules sit on top: the Reserve Bank requires payment system data to be stored only in India, and insurance, securities, telecom and health data carry their own conditions. Check the sector rule first, then the contract.
26-10.benefit: Section 16 of the 2023 Act deals with cross-border transfer and lets the government restrict a destination by notification. The Reserve Bank's 2018 direction on storage of payment system data requires the full payment data to be stored in India. Sector regulators, including IRDAI, SEBI, the Department of Telecommunications and the National Health Authority for ABDM, add their own localisation and cloud conditions. A transfer to a group company abroad is still a transfer.
26-10.cost: A data centre in India and a legal review cost money. A sector breach can cost the licence.
26-10.caveats: Do not assume a standard contractual clause is enough. Check the sector rule for the data you hold. Keep a record of what leaves India and where it goes.
26-10.sources: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, storage of payment system data. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; National Health Authority. <https://nha.gov.in/>

26-12.title: A data breach: contain it, tell the regulator, tell the users, and report a cyber incident to CERT-In within six hours
26-12.inPlainWords: If personal data is breached, lost or altered, contain it first. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 the data fiduciary must notify the Data Protection Board and each affected person, in the form and within the time the rules prescribe. Separately, CERT-In's 2022 directions require a cyber incident to be reported within six hours of noticing it, and the logs kept in India for 180 days. A cyber fraud or an intrusion should also go to cybercrime.gov.in or the 1930 helpline. Do not wait for a complete picture before filing the first report.
26-12.benefit: Section 8 of the 2023 Act makes notification of a breach to the Board and to the affected data principals a duty of the data fiduciary. CERT-In's directions of 28 April 2022 require reporting of specified cyber incidents within six hours and the maintenance of logs for 180 days in India. The Information Technology Act, 2000 gives CERT-In its power to call for information. Concealment is treated more seriously than the incident itself.
26-12.cost: An incident-response retainer and a forensic report cost money. A late report can cost a penalty.
26-12.caveats: Do not delete the logs. Do not tell users more than you know, and do not tell them less than the law requires. Keep one timeline of who knew what and when.
26-12.sources: CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

26-13.title: Auto-renewing subscriptions: give a pre-debit notice, make cancellation as easy as sign-up, and do not trap the user
26-13.inPlainWords: Before the first payment, say clearly that the subscription renews automatically, at what price and when. Before each recurring debit, the Reserve Bank's e-mandate framework requires a pre-debit notification to the customer, and the mandate needs an additional factor of authentication where the framework requires it. Give a cancellation route as easy to find as the sign-up button, and stop charging the moment it is used. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 a hidden renewal is an unfair trade practice, and the authority's dark-pattern guidelines call the subscription trap a dark pattern.
26-13.benefit: The Reserve Bank's framework for recurring e-mandates requires the customer to be told before a debit, requires the mandate to be authenticated, and requires a cancellation to be honoured. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 covers an unfair trade practice and a restrictive trade practice, and the Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 guidelines on dark patterns list the subscription trap as a prohibited design. The Indian Contract Act, 1872 governs the terms, and a term buried behind a link is weak.
26-13.cost: The reminder and the cancel button cost development time. A refund and a penalty cost more.
26-13.caveats: Do not bury the renewal in the terms. Do not make the user telephone you to cancel. Keep the cancellation confirmation and the pre-debit notices you sent.
26-13.sources: Reserve Bank of India, recurring e-mandates. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

26-11.cost: Cloud instances from major providers are billed monthly and cost noticeably more than a small VPS. VPS plans from smaller vendors are the cheap way to start. A VPS is essentially a virtual mini‑server. Dedicated server hosting also means you must purchase the hardware yourself.
26-11.inPlainWords: The main difference among these three options isn’t price — it’s what resources you’ll have at hand when something goes wrong. Big providers offer registration pathways, publish their credentials, issue outage notices, and include compensation clauses in their contracts, so help is readily available. Smaller vendors may charge half as much, but they often over‑sell capacity, disappear without notice, or get cut off by upstream providers; in such cases you won’t know who to turn to. For static websites that contain no user data, a cheap VPS is perfectly adequate.
26-11.benefit: Again, the key distinction isn’t price but the support you can rely on during an emergency. Major cloud providers provide registration channels, disclose their qualifications, announce any outages, and guarantee compensation under their contracts, ensuring you can get assistance when needed. Smaller vendors can offer prices roughly half of those rates, yet when they over‑sell resources, shut down unexpectedly, or lose upstream connectivity, you have no recourse. Therefore, before negotiating a price, verify who the vendor actually is: a company’s record can be checked on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs portal, a payment-related service’s authorisation with the Reserve Bank of India, and the terms it publishes in its contract. Dedicated server hosting only makes sense if two conditions are met: the bandwidth or hardware costs are noticeably lower, and you have in‑house staff capable of managing the server. For static sites without user data, the cheapest VPS is sufficient; for sites that handle user registrations and transactions, choose a cloud instance that offers elastic scaling and snapshot backups, and store those backups in at least two separate locations.
26-11.sources: Author’s experience, no direct documentation; see the entry on data security and breach reporting for breach-notification duties; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>
